chantedPrayers.text:
LIBERATING PRAYER

O Blessed One, Shakyamuni Buddha,
Precious treasury of compassion,
Bestower of supreme inner peace,
You who love all beings without exception
Are the source of happiness and goodness;
And you guide us to the liberating path.

Your body is a wish-fulfilling jewel,
Your speech is supreme, purifying nectar,
And your mind is refuge for all living beings.

With folded hands I turn to you,
Supreme unchanging friend,
I request from the depths of my heart:

Please give me the light of your wisdom
To dispel the darkness of my mind
And to heal my mental continuum.

Please nourish me with your goodness,
That I in time may nourish all beings
With an unceasing banquet of delight.

Through your compassionate intention,
Your blessings and virtuous deeds,
And my strong wish to rely upon you,
May all suffering quickly cease
And all happiness and joy be fulfilled;
And may holy Dharma flourish forevermore.

We should know that learning to cherish others is the best method for establishing world peace in general and for our own peace of mind in particular. If everyone sincerely prays to be able to cherish other living beings, then gradually, through the power of this prayer, everyone will actually cherish each other. The world will then be permanently at peace, and pure and everlasting happiness will pervade the entire world.

Understanding this, we recite the following prayers, while concentrating on their meaning.

PRAYER OF THE STAGES OF THE PATH

To attain the supreme peace of mind, enlightenment,
I make excellent offerings to the holy beings,
The enlightened beings of the ten directions
And the assembly of Bodhisattvas.

However many flowers and fruits there are,
In all the different types of medicine,
All the jewels there are in the world,
And all the pure refreshing waters,

Mountains of jewels, forest groves,
And quiet and joyful places,
Heavenly trees adorned with flowers,
And trees whose branches hang with delicious fruits,

Scents that come from the celestial realms,
Incense, wish-granting trees and jewel trees,
Harvest that need no cultivation,
And all ornaments there are suitable to be offered,

Lakes and pools adorned with lotuses,
And the beautiful call of wild geese,
Everything that is unowned throughout our world,
As extensive as space —

Holding these in my mind, I offer them well
To the supreme beings, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
O compassionate ones, holy objects of offering,
Think of me kindly and accept what I offer.

With the intention to attain the ultimate supreme goal
That surpasses even the wish-granting jewel,
May I constantly cherish all living beings.

Whenever I associate with others,
May I view myself as the lowest of all,
And with a pure intention
May I cherish others as supreme.

Examining my mental continuum
Throughout all my actions,
As soon as a delusion of self-cherishing develops
Whereby I or others would act inappropriately,
May I firmly face it and avert it.

Whenever I see unfortunate beings
Oppressed by evil and violent suffering,
May I cherish them as if I had found
A rare and precious treasure.

Even if someone I have helped
And of whom I had great hopes
Nevertheless harmed me intentionally,
May I see him or her as my holy spiritual guide.

When others out of jealousy or anger
Harm me or insult me,
May I take defeat upon myself
And offer them the victory.

In short, may I directly and indirectly
Offer help and happiness to all my mothers,
And secretly take upon myself
All their harm and suffering.

Furthermore, through all the above,
Free from the stains of the eight worldly concerns,
May I, recognizing all phenomena as like illusions,
Be released from the bondage of mistaken appearance and conception.

guidedMeditation.speaker: Kadam Kyle
guidedMeditation.text:
We can get into a comfortable posture. We can first begin by just remembering our great compassion. We have a strong wish to protect each and every living being. Just imagine or feel what this powerful mind is like — of great compassion.

Through reflecting on our great compassion, we realize that we are unable to help all living beings in this way at this moment. Therefore, we need to become a Buddha, so that we have the actual power and ability to truly be of benefit.

The truth of this becomes clear when we think about the attributes a true liberator of others must have. Such a being would have to possess the four characteristics of an awakened one: one, freedom from all obstructions preventing liberation and omniscience; two, great skill in liberating living beings from their suffering; three, compassion for all living beings without discrimination; and four, benefiting all living beings, whether or not they have helped him.

Reflect on these qualities. And through doing so, turn your mind of compassion into bodhichitta, thinking: I must become enlightened. I need these four qualities if I am to really benefit others.

That wish arises. We just hold that single-pointedly, deep in our heart.

In the last couple of minutes, just really imagine — or believe — that you've developed this mind of bodhichitta, thinking: I really want to benefit others. I need to become enlightened. If I become a Buddha, I can benefit each and every living being.

Then in our own time, while maintaining our bodhichitta, we can gradually rise from our practice.

postMeditation.speaker: Kadam Kyle
postMeditation.text:
Does anyone want to be our lucky duck reader of the Guide to the Bodhisattva's Way of Life? Anyone feeling festive today? Zesty, maybe, would be the best word.

Oh, sorry, Byron. Yes, we are now doing verses 26 to 36, please.

shantidevaReading.speaker: Byron
shantidevaReading.text:
(26) How can we possibly measure
The benefits of this jewel of a mind —
The source of joy for all living beings
And the cure for all their sufferings?

(27) If the mere intention to benefit others
Is more meritorious than making offerings to the Buddhas,
What can be said of actually striving
For the happiness of every single living being?

(28) Although living beings wish to be free from suffering,
They run straight towards the causes of suffering;
And although they wish for happiness,
Out of ignorance they destroy it like a foe.

(29) For those who are deprived of happiness
And afflicted with many sorrows,
Bodhichitta bestows upon them boundless joy,
Eradicates all their suffering,

(30) And even dispels their confusion.
Where is there virtue equal to this?
Where is there even such a friend?
Where is there merit such as this?

(31) If even someone who repays a kindness
Is worthy of some praise,
What can be said of the Bodhisattva who helps others
Regardless of whether or not they help him?

(32) If someone regularly, or even just once,
Gives food in a disdainful manner,
Which satisfies a few beings for only half a day,
People honour him or her as virtuous;

(33) So what can be said of one who eternally gives
To countless living beings
The everlasting, unsurpassed bliss of the Sugatas,
Fulfilling all their wishes?

(34) Buddha said that whoever generates an evil mind
Towards a Bodhisattva, a supreme benefactor,
Will remain in hell for as many aeons
As the moments for which that evil mind was generated;

(35) But, for whoever generates a pure mind of faith,
The effects of good fortune will increase even more than that.
Even when Bodhisattvas are faced with great adversity,
Negativity does not arise; rather, their virtues naturally increase.

(36) I prostrate to those who have generated
The holy, precious mind of bodhichitta;
And I go for refuge to those sources of happiness
Who bestow bliss even upon those who harm them.

postReading.speaker: Kadam Kyle
postReading.text:
Thank you very much, Byron. I feel like every time we do these verses, they get better and better every time. They're like sinking in slowly at least. Thank you very much, Byron, I appreciate it.

Okay, let's see. We were exploring all sorts of fun and wondrous things. We were looking at the vows of aspiring bodhichitta — you remember those? Some six times a day fun stuff, not abandoning living beings, not deceiving our spiritual guide, accumulating merit and wisdom, all that good stuff. So we were talking about that a little bit last week, and we talked about maybe people could take one and sort of mine it throughout the week and chew it over and put it into practice in some way.

We also looked at the four characteristics of a Buddha in the meditation — just kind of admiring them and finding them so beautiful that they push us forward on our journey to enlightenment. And whatever else we wanted to get up to over the week.

practiceReports.speaker: Anne
practiceReports.text:
I took as my aspiration not abandoning all living beings. And it made me much more mindful than usual. I think it just gave me a lot of incentive.

I was basically thinking about the fact that the world is a reflection of my mind. So anytime my mind was in a negative state, I was creating a negative world for everybody, not just me. So it made me super aware. I went to the gym and they have a new thing — you can't get in and scan your iPhone, and that wasn't working. So the lady had to come up and said, I could buy a key fob if that doesn't work, but that would cost me ten dollars. And typically I'd be like, yeah, and I would just perseverate on how ridiculous it was. And I'm like, no, I'm not going to do that.

Just little things like that. Whatever negative, critical view came into my mind, I was like, no, don't do it. Keep your mind positive, positive, positive, positive, no matter what. And I was able to do that this week to a degree that I hadn't been able to before. It seemed more fun to keep a positive mind than to engage in my usual shenanigans. And it felt fantastic. I had a really good week. It was kind of a challenging week in many ways. But it was super fun. So I was very happy with this — I'm definitely going to keep it up.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text:
Thanks, Anne! Fantastic. Yeah, I love that. The idea of not abandoning living beings — part of that means using our thoughts in kind and useful ways, because when we have a negative thought, it actually does harm others. And there are obvious ways where that is true, and then there are some subliminal ways that that's true.

Yeah, so it's a great objective, right? I want to be really sort of considerate about what my thoughts are doing throughout the day — not just for me, but for the people around me and how it affects them. Yeah, it's so great. I think Venerable Geshe-la had said once, be generous with your thoughts, something like that. Use your thoughts in a generous way. It's a really nice idea to kind of play around with. Thanks so much, Anne.

practiceReports.speaker: Sumit
practiceReports.text:
Mine is kind of simple. I was at the temple last week for a retreat. And, you know, there's a bunch I could say, but I think one thing that just — it's a simple thing — it was a silent retreat. My meditation practice really got a lot of material improvement. And it's so funny because we spend a lot of time trying to become better meditators and do things. And sometimes there's just some really simple hacks. If you go to the temple, things are better. If you go into silence, things are better. And, like, a lot better.

We have all these little things we do in our life to make things a little bit better. We want our food to taste a little bit better, so we add a little bit of salt. We do those little things and it becomes a lot better. And I just want to throw that out — it's almost like an endorsement for something I think we all know. But just to add my extra two cents: how much of a big difference it makes. Go to the temple, go into silence. We all need this. If we're about this, at some point in our year we should try to really emphasize making some time to do some retreat.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text:
Thanks, Sumit. Yeah, it's kind of two points. One is just the magic of the temple itself, and two, it's about retreat and the benefits of it.

And yeah, we can do our best with retreat. Some people have conditions where it's very difficult to actually get out and go somewhere. But you can create a retreat at home, or retreat conditions, or at least a more retreat-ish condition if it's not physically possible. There are steps we can do, and we don't have to be totally all or nothing. For example, having a retreat-like evening once in a while, or a retreat-like morning, or maybe a Saturday block where we have a little bit of space. There are ways to integrate.

And even mental retreat — mental retreat is one of the three types of retreat. We can actually be on mental retreat anytime. We can't always be on physical retreat, separating ourselves from our ordinary activities. And we can't always be on verbal retreat unless we're incredibly mindful of our speech. But we can actually be on mental retreat. And sometimes I've found even in commuting, I'm on retreat while just going through my life. All of a sudden everything is a billion times better.

Anyway, that's just a point about retreat in general — and of course if we can create a week or a weekend, it's worth so much. But if we can't, there are ways to have something approaching a more retreat-like experience.

And then your point about the temple specifically — yeah, there is something that is a little bit unmatchable about the blessed space of the temple. I get to do the presiding at Wish-Fulfilling Jewel at the temple a lot. The ones I preside here have zero time because they're fit into a small block. But the Wish-Fulfilling Jewels I do at the temple are always like five times better than any meditation I can do normally — even though it's just chanted prayers. There's zero time to even be quiet. But it's the power of the blessed space. Our guru walked every inch of this place. The temple is basically Heruka's pure land. So it's a good place to hang out and meditate, even if we've got not much going on mentally.

practiceReports.speaker: Fran
practiceReports.text:
So I've been in a sort of slump — a seated meditation slump. And I have to admit that the TTP homework assignments could not have been further from my mind this week. I turned around and said, oh, I haven't even taken out my books. Yesterday I said, oh, there are those four characteristics that Kadam Kyle told us. I'll memorize them. All right, tomorrow morning I'll do that. And I did take it out and make a feeble attempt this morning.

But I have been doing the six sessions, and I'm so grateful for that. And one part of my six sessions is to remember that Geshe-la is always at my heart. And that's really — for me, that's been the most important thing. And everything else will come from that. I just feel confident that the seated practice will come back. Even just being in today — I have my shrine here and I haven't been in this room all week to even sit in front of my shrine. But the six sessions I've been doing that religiously, with a little bit of other bits and pieces here and there. And that's been carrying me through.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Thank you, Fran. That's one of the many special qualities of having a structure like that — a baseline practice. Even if other things are a little up in the air and a little all over the place, we have something that's like a bedrock in our practice and in our mind that keeps the continuum going. It really doesn't matter what that thing is. It could be one second that we do each day. There's no rule about it being too minimal. So the six sessions is a nice aim, but whatever it is, is great. And you're just demonstrating the value of that. Yeah, thank you.

practiceReports.speaker: Suzanne
practiceReports.text:
So this week I was feeling a flare-up from last week. And somehow I had to teach Tom's class, and I'd never really taught a class before — I kind of led his class with discussion. And I didn't know what the topic was until the night before, and I couldn't prepare because my head was pounding. So I just kind of did the best I could and gave a very, very short teaching. I don't even know what I said. And we had a nice discussion, and I led a meditation — which always seems weird since we had that one teaching skills class where you kind of made me overthink it. I didn't think before that I could lead a meditation. But now they seem to like it, so I'm going to have to work on that.

But I just wanted to share that, you know, despite the fact that I really hate public speaking — I kind of did it. I realize I'm doing it right now. But I still don't like it. So that's it.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Could you say — what did you get from the experience?

practiceReports.speaker: Suzanne
practiceReports.text: A headache. It doesn't make me want to rush back and do it again. I'm in better physical condition, perhaps. I don't know. But I figured that Tom needs the break. He needs to know he's backed up. And yeah, so I felt like I kind of had to do it. We'll try it again sometime — I'll report back.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: It was probably spiritually more meaningful than if you had not done it. Would you agree?

practiceReports.speaker: Suzanne
practiceReports.text: Maybe. But it's like two days later I forgot that I did it already. So it's like, it doesn't stick.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text:
Well, you remember now. So that's good.

In the future I would be very happy to know whenever someone is teaching — especially for the first time. I would really like to know, just so I could support you and root you on. Anyway, thank you very much.

practiceReports.speaker: Anne P
practiceReports.text:
So since I started in TTP, I've been working on one subject in my meditation — my seated meditation — which is opening my heart. Okay, so my dog died ten days ago. So I meditate now with my dog beside me.

My heart is open. And it feels good. I also visualize Vajrayogini coming through my head. And I'm kind of adjusted to my dog being dead. But I find that visualizing her presence next to me is helpful.

So, what I do is I open my heart and then I do taking and giving. I have a lot of sick, aging friends and relatives, and I do every day like a half hour of taking and giving for these people. And it's very good. I find my heart is definitely open. And it's not just sadness — when I meditate I'm not sad. I'm sad sharing it because it's close to me. But when I meditate I'm not typically sad — I'm happy. So that's just what I wanted to share.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text:
It's really nice that you could share that. And yeah, it's a good reminder that whenever we meditate, we try to remember our family and friends closest to us — everyone's family, because they're people, right? And this means people who are living on this earth or living in another realm. Because there's no actually dead people, right? You don't technically die. You just change your appearance. You leave one body and go to another. So you're never actually gone.

So we can feel in the presence of those who have passed from this world when we meditate every time. And it's really nice — especially our family and friends closest to us. As you kind of demonstrated, it's very powerful for opening up our heart. Yeah, thank you, Anne. Anyone else want to share anything?

practiceReports.speaker: Kristin
practiceReports.text:
I will say — it was the winter break, and I had a conference right before. So I was at West, and then Grady and the kids came, and we went to some national parks — Joshua Tree and Death Valley.

And I will say that I was doing a lot of dedication because I was just really kind of blown away by the experience. I just felt like it was more than I could handle. It was just incredible. And having the opportunity to be in a place like that, and be outdoors experiencing such a different climate and wildlife and everything — it was just overwhelming. And I also hadn't seen these guys for a couple of days. So I just felt like I was exploding, in a good way. But I was like, I'm dedicating this, I'm dedicating this. I think it was one of the first times I remembered it so early to dedicate all of the positivity. And I was like, this is karma ripening. And I was kind of worrying about the fact that I was ripening all this good karma that I need. But I was dedicating it for all of you and for everyone really, because it felt very liberating and very joyful and very expansive.

And also — we are so tiny. And our perspective is so — just getting so dramatically out of your day-to-day makes it easier to see how limited it is and how kind of crazy it is.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Yeah, it makes a lot of sense, Kristin — the not just the contrast of the difference, right, from Nyack to Death Valley, but the vastness of that space, and not being in the same rigmarole of our normal life. It can just give us a little bit of room to change our perspective. Maybe not get caught up in it all.

practiceReports.speaker: Grady
practiceReports.text:
It really does give you this sense of scale. You become so small. It's incredible. And we did like a very physical kind of exchanging — being at the top of a viewpoint at 5,075 feet above, and then being down below sea level, kind of reflecting back up. Just completely different. So to kind of bring that into your practice and exchanging self and others and kind of your perspective.

And we also said a lot of mantras — a lot of Tara mantras, because there was some extreme wind and we were in an RV and weren't exactly sure if it was going to topple over. So we were awake at two o'clock in the morning, each of us on our own. The next morning we were creating an escape plan a little bit, but then it kind of died down at about three o'clock in the morning. The next morning I was like, I was definitely doing mantras, and Chris was like, oh man, me too. So we were definitely using the method.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: That's very nice. Thank you all. I'm glad that Death Valley didn't earn its name while you were there. And that you guys could just kind of mix Dharma with the trip. And that's probably partially why it was so delightful. Yeah, thank you.

mainTeaching.speaker: Ben
mainTeaching.text:
I have a question — it's actually from a few classes ago. You were talking about with the meditation about how all living beings are mothers. Something that we sometimes helpfully advise — if it's not working for someone — is, okay, if the mother thing isn't working, you can try something else that does work, something easier. And I think what you said was, if we're going to be serious about this though, let's do the actual practice — so whatever it is making that not work, maybe get over it.

So I was thinking about it. And I realized I just don't know what that means for me. To volunteer: my current life, the mother I have is not the issue. All the things that it says in the book, she did. So that's not the problem. I do feel like I have spent a lot of time taking that advice to, okay, if this doesn't work, do something else. But there's no obviously identifiable obstacle I can see that explains why this just doesn't produce the feeling that is described.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
Yeah, it's a really nice question, Ben. And a very practical, useful question that could probably apply to any meditation. It's like, hmm, I'm doing this meditation and it's just not grooving for me. And so then it's like, how do we kind of run a diagnostic on that? How do we figure out what's going on? Because generally speaking, if it was obvious about what's going on, we would just probably fix it and not have it go on. So usually when we have a challenge with a meditation, or it just doesn't spark something in us like maybe other ones do, then there's an obvious challenge but it's hiding a little bit. So how do we kind of systematically identify what those obstacles might be?

This is a really important skill — to do this with all the meditations, especially all the Lamrim meditations, to kind of go through one by one. It takes time, it takes years. But, like: do I have a spark with this one? Do I feel like a blessing when I think about this meditation, where I'm just so delighted when I think about it? When I go to a teaching on it, am I jumping for joy? And the answer is no. Okay, great, that's fine. But then I want to figure out what's going on beneath the surface. So maybe I can offer a couple of ideas — these are more general ideas about this process, and hopefully they relate to this specific meditation.

The first is asking: what's the joyful, virtuous experience this meditation leads to? This is a big obstacle buster, because sometimes when we have an obstacle with a meditation, our conception of the object is something that's diametrically opposed to the actual object of meditation. And especially if it somehow seems related to some unpleasant experience we've had in this life or know about, then we kind of map that unpleasant experience onto the meditation, even though it's not naturally part of it. So for example, with the mother meditation, maybe we have an unpleasant experience of dutifully having to do things for others because we're supposed to — out of guilt or pressure. So it could be that we map that experience onto this meditation as if that's somehow related to the object. Which sounds horrible, right? That's not the object. That's not the joyful experience. So that's one area always worth pondering: what exactly is the virtuous, joyful experience of the meditation supposed to be? Because a virtuous mind is a joyful, peaceful mind. There are no delusions at that moment.

The second kind of diagnostic tool is asking: what are my personal obstacles around this topic? Obviously with mother-related things, it could be a very obvious one. In your case, maybe not. But for some people, it could be. For example, practicing patience — some people have an obstacle because someone abused them in their life, and so they hear the teaching on patience as, you're saying I should basically take it, I should put up with abuse. That issue isn't actually the meditation of patience — it's an unresolved experience that's making them misunderstand the meaning of patience. And so it's actually a different challenge. That's the obstacle.

With the mother meditation, there's also the obstacle of pride — we don't want to feel reliant on other people. There's something that feels awful about being reliant on others. This is an American issue especially. And part of this meditation is saying, we were completely powerless, we would have died if it wasn't for our mother, we owe it all to her. That might feel threatening to a sense of, I'm independent, I've earned this, I've done this. Instead of thinking, no, this is beautiful that I'm completely dependent on my mother and her generosity and her mercy. So that would be another example of an obstacle — a kind of diluted pride around a false sense of independence.

And then the third one for now would be asking: what are the specific problems that this meditation solves that I cannot solve without it? Why is this one drawn out specifically in the Lamrim so carefully, when so many other meditations were left in the background? And it's because it solves specific inner problems that are quite difficult to solve in any other way. That's a really fun question, because then we can get into the logic of it. Like, ooh, that's why this meditation's here.

For me, that's what got me into the death meditation originally — because I didn't really have an overt issue with it, but it just wasn't moving me. And it wasn't until I was in the throes of craving, and reading that section, and really getting punished by a craving mind — that I read through it and went, oh, without this meditation, I cannot solve my craving problem. And I was like, I want to solve my craving problem so badly, and this is the meditation, do it. And then all of a sudden the meditation worked, because I became really aware, intricately, of why it's there and what it does.

So those are a couple of ideas on how we might approach a meditation like this — any time we're coming up to a Lamrim object and we're not getting that spark.

mainTeaching.speaker: Ben
mainTeaching.text: Yeah, yeah. And the last suggestion in particular — I hadn't thought of that and I wonder if that could be a worthwhile one.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text: Yeah, I think so. Sometimes what happens is that we end up having a problem later on with another Lamrim meditation, and then we can reverse-engineer it back to an earlier Lamrim object and go, oh, I've been having a problem with this other one that I actually like, but it's all because of my mother one — it's all messed up. And that kind of gives us the sense of, okay, I've got to dig into this one. That happens a lot with people's renunciation, or the fear of lower rebirth meditation, or karma meditation, or even precious human life meditation. They get into the highest secret tantra and elaborate, amazing meditations, but they hit a ceiling they can't break through. And it's like, oh, that's why this meditation's here. I guess I've got to put my boots on and march into the danger of the lower rebirth area of the Lamrim again and revisit that, because I tried to skip it a little bit, and now I'm facing the consequences of skipping an essential nutrient for our mind. Okay, good. Thanks, Ben, for raising that point.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
So we're in, we got through the eight precepts. Now we're on to the benefits of the aspiring mind.

It has been said that if we were to offer a universe full of jewels to the fully enlightened beings, the merit created would be great indeed. However, Buddha Shakyamuni has said that the merit that arises merely from the mind that seeks enlightenment for the benefit of others is thousands of times greater than this. Such an aspiring mind overcomes the disadvantages and hindrances of samsara, and outshines the qualities of those spiritual practitioners — the so-called Hearers and Solitary Conquerors — who work only for their own liberation. As great as these benefits are, however, an uninterrupted flow of merit does not arise from the aspiring mind in the way that it does from the engaging mind.

From the time when the complete Bodhisattva vows are taken with the fearless mind that never turns back from its task of freeing all sentient beings from their suffering and leading them to enlightenment, great and unimaginable merit arises. The merit of such a mind is much greater than that which arises from the aspiring mind, and it comes even when the Bodhisattva is asleep, unconcerned, or apparently intoxicated. Moreover, whatever actions of body, speech, and mind the person possessing this engaging mind undertakes become the cause for their eventual attainment of the highest and most perfect enlightenment.

There are two types of reasoning that establish the immense benefits of bodhichitta: reasoning from scripture and from logic. As for the former — in Sutra Requested by Subahu, Buddha himself listed the many benefits of developing bodhichitta. Why was this teaching given? In order to persuade those who were inclined to the Hinayana path, which leads only to our own liberation from suffering, to follow the Mahayana path, which leads to full enlightenment for the sake of others.

The reasoning from logic establishing the benefits of bodhichitta follows from the observation that in general there are many types of virtuous or beneficial intentions we might have. For instance, a mother has a beneficial intention towards her child, and we may have a beneficial intention towards the poor and needy. But the beneficial intention of a Bodhisattva, whose great compassion extends to all living beings, is much greater than either of these examples.

The extensive and unsurpassable benefits of bodhichitta are illustrated by the following story taken from a previous life of Buddha Shakyamuni. This is a real classic — this is a good one to read in general program class when you have it.

It is related that in a particular lifetime he created much negative karma by fighting with his mother and stepping over her head as she lay on the floor trying to block his departure. As a result of such a heavy non-virtuous action he was reborn in a hellish state of existence. In that karmically-created realm he had to endure the continual and excruciating suffering of having his head bored into. By what? Is it like flesh-eating bugs? Is it drills? Anyways — something terrible, I'm sure. Around him were other beings who were all experiencing the same torment. The sight of these suffering beings stirred something within the boy's heart. Implanted on his mind was the karmic imprint of a previous beneficial intention, and when this arose in response to the others' torment, he prayed: 'How wonderful it would be if all sentient beings were separated from all pains inflicted on their heads; may all such suffering ripen upon me!' This is taking and giving, right? This is teaching taking and giving.

Such was the power of this beneficial intention that all of the negative karma he had collected from harming his mother was completely purified. Immediately he was reborn in a god realm.

I think our kids' class in the future would be very popular if we taught this to the children. And the parents would be very happy that we set the children straight. So anyway, the parents here can confirm whether that's true. But they would be very well behaved, I think, if they knew about the situation. Yeah, it's fantastic.

Shantideva uses the example of the great merit that arises from a beneficial intention directed merely at relieving the suffering of others' headaches as a standard of comparison. The merit from such a limited intention is so great — what need is there to speak about the limitless merits of a Bodhisattva's pure intention? For his intention, deriving from his bodhichitta motivation, is to separate all sentient beings from all their suffering and lead them to the highest state of enlightenment. The Bodhisattva works not only to bring sentient beings temporary happiness, but also to lead them to the ultimate happiness of Buddhahood.

Does even our father or mother have the same beneficial intention as the Bodhisattva has towards us? No. It is true that our kind father and mother want to dispel our temporary suffering and give us temporary happiness, but it does not occur to them to wish us the sublime joyful state of full awakening, the complete cessation of all our suffering.

Okay, so this is just getting at the same point — but it's a mind-blowing point. Which is just the true power of the mind and mental actions. And this is something we can all work on improving. I know I can improve it. I'm sure we can all take this forward. Probably not until we're a Buddha do we have the full understanding of the power of mental actions.

It's a little bit like Anne's point earlier in the data sharing — okay, I don't want to abandon any living being, I'm going to be very mindful of every thought. And it's also related to when we looked at karma and the laws of karma a few weeks ago, but the power of our thoughts to create effects. So to me, when I'm reading this section — because it's a very long set of ideas that are just making this exact point over and over and over again — mental actions are so powerful. What we do with our mind is so powerful. And I'm going, what does that mean for me in my practice? Do I believe in the power of mental actions? Do I really have faith in the power of my mind to solve the problems of my life and of the world and of samsara? Do I understand how that works intellectually? Do I understand how that works experientially? Do I really believe in the power of mental actions?

Because of course we do believe in the power of physical actions to some degree. But the Buddhist approach is that mental actions are basically millions of times more powerful. So it's an utter inversion of our normal way of thinking. People say this to the Buddhist center a lot: you people aren't actually helping anyone, come on, what are you doing all day? But the Buddhist approach is that no, our mental actions are infinitely powerful. They're undoing samsara as a whole. And if one little action can create a whole new realm — right, Buddha just wishing people to be free of their headaches can remove a hell realm and appear a pure realm — that one action could do that. What about all of our mental actions that we use in our life?

So it's kind of like trying to get the sense that inside each and every one of us there's something so powerful. It's like — with AI and these kind of things right now, people are building data centers that are like the size of cities, to basically create a mind. They're making a city that sucks in the electricity of a small country just to try to make a mind. But each one of us has one of those already — and more than what they can create — inside of our heart. So to me it's actually a helpful image. Like, wow, the whole world's going crazy, all this wealth and money and time is going in for this one aim because they think it's so powerful. But we have that exact power and more, times a billion, in our clear light mind, in our root mind, out of our heart. We have it inside of us. This incredible power.

So it's like, what would it be like every day when we wake up and we think: my mind is like a world builder. My mind is a realm builder. It can create a realm — basically an entire reality — with a thought. Wow, that's a powerful force. Much more powerful than any technology I can see. Wow, my mind can turn an enemy into a kind mother. Nothing else out there can do that. Diplomacy can't do that — it's not going very well in the world. All these clever diplomats, they can't turn an enemy into a kind mother. It's only the mind that can do that. The mind can turn poison into nectar. The mind can turn us into a Buddha. It's unbelievably potent and powerful.

So this is what I was really getting from this section. Just thinking: mental actions are so potent, they're so powerful. And just trying to get the sense of — okay, how can I increase my faith in the power of mental actions?

And in the next session after the break, I'd love to hear from people: how can we as a group, as a TTP Sangha, increase our faith in the power of mental actions? It could be through logic. It could be through experience. It could be through certain teachings. But I think if we get that, then naturally we'll get the sense of: wow, bodhichitta is obviously the most powerful mental action. So therefore, if mental actions are already basically world builders, and bodhichitta is the most pure mental action, then of course I want to cultivate bodhichitta. It's like a natural cause and effect relationship that will develop.

So maybe you can think about that while you eat your ramen noodles — or whatever you're going to do over our little break.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Okay, so as I said in the last session — it'd be nice just to hear, maybe just for ten minutes or so. How can we increase our faith and understanding of the power of mental actions?

teaching.speaker: David
teaching.text: So as I was contemplating this, I kept coming back to the Buddha Shakyamuni saying that you should know that all phenomena are like dreams. Consider — in a dream, if you experience a bunch of stuff, people suffering, people having good experiences, you're able to change your mind in that dream. Everything is on the table. Things can change very quickly. And actually, in some sense, I feel like there are no physical or verbal actions really in a dream. If you do something good in a dream, is that really a physical action, or is that a mental action? And even in this waking world, if we accept there is a difference — it's like all of our physical and verbal actions are preceded by mental actions anyway. Every single thing we experience ultimately, from a karmic standpoint, is coming from a mental action. And the way we experience it is all mental too.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Yeah, those are two good points — thinking of phenomena like dreams, and then even verbal and physical actions being principally influenced by mind.

teaching.speaker: Anne
teaching.text: For me, I think the only way to generate faith in mental actions is to stop taking any other kind of action as much as possible. So if I'm having difficulty with a situation, the first thing to do is try to purify it. Or if I'm having trouble with a person, the first thing to do is imagine them as completely pure and what they would be like. And actually saying something or doing something has to be the last resort. It's hard to live that way. There are a lot of things I don't have the capacity yet to transform. But the more I make that the first step in solving any problem, the more I grow my ability to do that, and the more I create faith in the ability to do that.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
Yeah, makes sense. Thanks, Anne. So you're kind of pointing out the difference between inner problems and outer problems. Step one: try to solve the inner problem just through changing the mind. Step two: deal with whatever is there if we've still got to deal with it. But we've got to do the order in the right way.

It is important, because it's like if you're a scientist trying to study the causality between a medicine and its healing properties, you don't want too many variables. You kind of want a control group — same kind of people, just plus the medicine. Not the medicine plus a different diet plus a different health regimen plus a little meditation practice, because then you've got seven variables and it's hard to distinguish what actually made the change. So it is a good point about doing these little experiments. Can I just solve the problem by changing my mind? And if we understand that problems are inner problems principally, then the answer is a resounding yes. Yeah, thank you. Sumit, yes.

teaching.speaker: Sumit
teaching.text:
What I would have to say kind of circles around what you're talking about with this inner and outer problem issue. So — if I'm honest, I don't think mental intentions have... the original question was kind of about developing faith that our mental intentions can be effective, right? So, I don't have faith that my mental intention is as powerful as my bodily actions in the external world. I don't think I can turn something into nectar through my mind. I could do it through a chemical process though.

But the thing is, it goes back to that point a little bit — I don't have faith that changing the external world will affect my internal world. So to me, it's not that I think the mental intention is more powerful than external actions in the external world. But that doesn't matter, because that's not what really matters. What really matters is the inner problems, my inner situation. And I do believe that mental intentions are more powerful than external actions when it comes to changing my inner world. And that's what does matter. That's what is actually my life, my experience.

You made this point about someone's enemy, right? I could change my mind and label this person as a friend or as an enemy. Changing my mind changes my inner world, but it might be less effective for curtailing their negative actions. I have this all the time as a teacher — the kids aren't exactly my enemies, but I'm trying to oppose their negative actions. Changing my mind to be okay with what they're doing changes how I perceive it, but it doesn't actually suppress their external behavior. I can take external actions to influence their behavior. So that's kind of my take.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
Yeah, gotcha. It's an interesting kind of point you're raising — that ultimately the power comes from solving the internal problem. Yeah. But this is where I think it could get a little bit muddled around what exactly is the external situation. Because the external situation is strictly perceived, right? It's strictly perceived. There's no external situation that is unperceived. So the enemy is a perceived enemy.

This is where we have to ponder it a little bit closely. By changing our internal state, I think our external state will also shift, because it's just an appearance to mind. Simply an appearance. If our internal state could change to a completely peaceful, wise state, and our external state looked completely as ordinary as before, that would mean those things were not an appearance to mind — it would mean they're inherently ordinary in some way. So I think we have to ponder it a little bit closely. But I do think your point is well taken, that the main idea is to solve the internal problem. That's the main idea.

teaching.speaker: Mary Ann
teaching.text:
I was trying to find something more grandiose, but I do have this relationship with someone that's been very long-term, and I really have been trying to apply equalizing self and others — thinking of her as I, trying some of those techniques that were mentioned in maybe the toolbox class. And now I just find myself being like, why did I ever want to censor or curb this person's freedom of expression or just not listen and be like, oh, okay, sure.

My lack of expectation — what I really thought I wanted from the interaction — it totally kind of fell away into just being like, yes, just love this person. They're so lovable. What was I thinking? I was using them mentally in a way to satisfy my own agendas of what I thought was fun, interesting, stimulating, meaningful — which in fact wasn't really the case. It was more like what was happening about the love feeling, and allowing them to do what they wanted to do and just accepting it.

So it's a small scale thing, but I definitely saw that my mind changed that person's level of kind of peace and happiness regarding our interaction. So it was really good.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Thanks, Mary Ann. Yeah, it's a nice illustration of the power of mental actions. And again, it's a little bit like this relationship between the inner and outer problems. We shift our mind and we just see there was no problem where it really felt like there was some serious drama going on, something we needed to fix and adjust and control. And it was a very nice feeling to completely let go of that. That's the power of the mind — just through practicing exchanging or equalizing self and others, some expectations fall away. Oh, now I'm more at peace with the relationship. Yeah, and everyone needs to know that.

teaching.speaker: Student
teaching.text:
I was just going to share that I was thinking about when Genla Dekyong came to visit us, and people asked lots of different questions — I have this problem with my meditation, I have this problem with being inspired. And every answer was — she said it so beautifully and so gently without judging — but basically she was like, the problem is that you think it's a problem. Just stop thinking it's a problem.

And I really feel like that was a big blessing we all got. Because I think sometimes I can spend a whole day — I visualize this pasta sieve, or a butterfly net — just like, oh, problem, problem, problem. And then, this is the problem. We can have whole relationships based on, oh yeah, because this is what the problem is. We're just experts. We can spend our whole life just articulating problems. But if you have even a little taste of what Mary Ann was saying, it's like, oh, there's no problem. So cool. And even if it's a trivial or superficial thing, it's the same process for the big ones. It's really cool.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Yeah, thank you, Adriana. It's just showing part of the power of the mind is to impute, right? And it imputes problem or opportunity or whatever. And if we could just notice that, our life would be about a billion times easier in the moment. It's just my mind imputing the problems that I'm running around obsessing about. And I don't necessarily need to do that if I don't want to.

teaching.speaker: Fran
teaching.text: It's basically the same thing. I was just thinking that we don't — to just look for the small things. If you're going to start building a foundation, like Mary Ann was saying, she was looking for something more grandiose. But if we're looking to be able to work in every situation, it's not going to happen immediately. Just find and notice the small things, and build from there.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Yeah, thanks, Fran. Have a gradual, incrementalist approach with our practice. And this is also related to the power of the mind — the little tiny thoughts can germinate and lead to huge cosmic changes in our life. Yeah, thank you.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
Okay, so I think we are at, in general, ordinary beings. Yeah, I think we stopped there. So:

In general, ordinary beings like ourselves, although we are filled with self-cherishing, strive only for the temporary happiness of this one life. We have no intention to attain the highest state of enlightenment, or even happiness for our future lives. Neither do we have the intention to find release from the sufferings of a hellish rebirth or from the sufferings of samsara as a whole. If the beneficial intention to be released from all suffering and attain enlightenment never arises for our own sake, not even in our dreams, then how will it ever arise for the sake of others? If we have no wish to be free from samsara ourselves, then how will the wish arise for others to be free from samsara?

If we meditate deeply by considering the constant suffering to which we are subjected, we can develop the wish to be liberated from all the unsatisfactory states that make up samsara. This wish to be free is called 'renunciation.' If we reflect on the sufferings of those who are in the same situation as ourselves, and realize that all sentient beings are suffering throughout samsara, the wish will arise that they also be freed. This is the development of true compassion, which leads to the generation of the bodhichitta wish.

Okay, so we understand this I think — but it's making an important point, and it's an important point for us as teachers too. There's a nice analogy here. If you were trying to cross a river and there was an opaque fog where you could barely see a foot in front of you — maybe you would just see one stone in the river to cross it. And then when you stepped on that one stone, you would see a second stone, because you can only see about a foot in front of you. And then on the second stone, you can see a third stone. And so there are certain types of knowledge, right, that are experiential like this, where they stack insofar as you gain one insight — and it's only through getting that insight that the next one even appears as possible. And then it's only through getting that one that the following insight only appears as possible.

So from the shore, that third stone is invisible. Completely invisible. Yeah, maybe someone could describe it to us — it's like this and it's like that — but it's still completely opaque. The fog is masking it. It's only when we step onto that second stone that it reveals itself. So a lot of Buddhist experience is like this — it's experience-dependent. Our understanding is experience-dependent. Of course there are words in the book, but they're not the experience at all. They're barely related. They're just like a map.

So with a lot of these meditations — in this case bodhichitta — bodhichitta is one of the little stones. But that stone only appears once we step on the stone of great compassion. And that stone really only appears in reality when we step on the stone of renunciation. It's essentially invisible what great compassion really means until our renunciation is powerful. And it's a bit invisible, actually, what bodhichitta means, until our great compassion is visible and powerful inside of us.

So from a teaching point of view — it's just a nice thing to think about when we're teaching a class. Am I just sitting on the shore going, wow, it's awesome out here, look at this tenth stone, everyone, it's so cool? Or am I really taking people to that first one for them, and then to that second one for them? Of course we do need to occasionally go, that tenth stone is awesome — wow, you've got to cross that river, baby — it's possible and it's great. A little big picture stuff, right. But from a practical point of view, it's completely invisible until that person takes that first step, then that second step, then that third step. If they're just sitting on the shore going, I know a lot about the tenth and eleventh stone, let me tell you about that — they're still just in the same place they always were.

So it's just a nice point to ponder whenever we're teaching Dharma. Are we really leading people and guiding people onto that next step in their practice? It's a little hard to know exactly what that is for them, but if we really put an intention in our heart to do that — and we ask our spiritual guide to help us — then we'll come up with some nice answers, strategies, and techniques.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
Now, when we're talking about the power of mental actions, I think David alluded to karma a little bit — but part of this is understanding merit. The power of merit. Because the mind is what creates merit, and it's because of merit that our mind is so powerful. And we want to remember what the definition of merit is.

When Geshe-la talked about real good fortune — what is real good fortune? He said — this is from the Mirror of Dharma teachings — merit means real good fortune, which technically means the cause of spiritual realizations. Not a good job, not high position, not favorable external circumstances. Those things are not merit. Whether external good fortune is even beneficial depends entirely on whether it leads to spiritual realizations. Without that, it could be a curse from one point of view — a distraction from what really matters.

Geshe-la's name itself means basically 'ocean of good fortune,' which is like merit ocean. And it's like, ah, that's real good fortune. It made his name very clear.

To understand the scope of a Bodhisattva's activity and to realize how powerful are the results of his or her motivation, consider the following. If we have a beneficial intention towards one hundred beings, then one hundred merits will arise. Similarly, if our beneficial intention is directed towards one thousand beings, then one thousand merits will arise. If this beneficial intention is directed towards countless beings, then the merits that arise will also be countless. Therefore the fruits that arise from the bodhichitta motivation are limitless. Because the object of bodhichitta is the countless sentient beings inhabiting the universe.

Someone might say that a Bodhisattva does not need to dispel the sufferings of sentient beings because they will do this by themselves. But in fact, ordinary beings are completely ignorant of the law of actions and their effects. Therefore, although they all wish to be free from misery, they nevertheless run straight towards it — which they do by their constant and ignorant creation of non-virtue, the very cause of their suffering. Similarly, although they wish for nothing but happiness, they systematically destroy virtue, the cause of happiness, as if it were their worst enemy.

We're not going to muddle the waters too much here, but we can ask ourselves: does my feeling that my mind creates the world, and that I'm responsible for my mind — does that feeling leak into a view that therefore other people are responsible for their minds, and therefore it's their job to deal with it? So there's an interesting kind of thing. I'm not sure it's easy to hold both views at once and see that they're not contradictory.

Both of these things are true: my mind is the creator of my world, and I am 100% responsible for all my happiness and suffering. All coming from mind. 100% responsible — no one else is responsible for it. It's my job. All I have to do is change my mind. And at the same time: other people — we are also responsible for them too. So those two things are not contradictory. They can seem contradictory, but they're not.

One thing that helps me personally: yes, I'm entirely responsible for my life and my world and my mind. But it is simply due to someone else painstakingly working to help me — spreading the Dharma, teaching and guiding — that I have an opportunity to do this. From my lived experience, if it wasn't for other people who were trying to help me, I would have no access to this. And simultaneously — my happiness is entirely dependent on my mind, and it's my job to deal with that. And it's like we're trying to see how these two things are not contradictory. And we need to be that person for someone else too. We need to be the person that they meet. If they don't meet someone, they're not going to have access to the liberating path.

In short, sentient beings do not know the method to attain freedom from suffering. They are deprived of happiness and always afflicted by pain and sorrow. It is the Bodhisattva who, by the power of the precious bodhichitta, dispels their suffering and leads them to happiness. Therefore, where is there a virtue comparable to bodhichitta — the mind of enlightenment that dispels the confusion of all beings, eradicates their suffering, and bestows upon them boundless joy? Where is there a friend equal to the precious bodhichitta who accomplishes all benefit and prevents all harm? Where is there merit similar to that of the mind of enlightenment?

So maybe each one of us can think about a little bit — how can we take this forward? A lot of this is incredible admiration for bodhichitta. We want to be asking: how can I take this with me into my life with what I'm dealing with in the week ahead, on the ground, with my life and my problems?

One nice way to do this — and this will be the last bit before discussion — is to try to get the real texture of our daily life and our lived experience when we're pondering a Dharma teaching like this. This is kind of how we figure out what that step is that we want to take, for us. It's a little bit like if you were a humanitarian aid worker in some war-torn area. You wouldn't just parachute in and say, all right, I'm here to help. You'd have a clear sense of: this is exactly the environment I'm entering. This is the terrain. These are the actual situations. Where are the easy wins? What's actually needed for the people here?

So with our own life — it's an interesting thing to do as a Dharma practitioner. Because we sort of have: I've been practicing all these years, I've been doing all these great things, I have these amazing practices and great spiritual experiences that I've tasted. And that's one thing. But it might be a bit opposed to: what's the actual texture of our lived life? And if that's the case, then our practice is going to be very abstract and generalized and not really relevant.

So the idea: I think a week at a time is very nice. What we're trying to do is get the terrain. What are the exact delusions that mess me up day to day? And amidst them, what are the easy wins? Like a humanitarian mission — okay, there's a simple blockage in the well. I can just unblock it. Easy win. It's not going to solve all the problems, but it's definitely a problem I can fix.

What's important when we do this is to not think anything is too small to work on. Actually especially keep an eye out for the little tiny petty delusions that happen in the day — minor annoyance, little craving moments, little non-acceptances. That area is so rich for growth. What would it be like to have no minor non-acceptance in the week ahead? Fantastic day. We'd be blissful actually I think if we completely unraveled all of our little minor non-acceptances, our little resistances of, I don't like it like this, I wish it was a little bit like that. If we unraveled that, it would actually be a blissful week. So when we're doing this, don't think anything is too small or trivial or whatever. That's often a place where we can get easy wins.

And then finally, what we want to do is just be clear — what's the actual Dharma tool? If it's not bodhichitta, maybe it's great compassion. If it's not great compassion, maybe it's wishing love. If it's not wishing love, maybe it's exchanging self with others. Or seeing all beings as a mother. Or affectionate love. Or equanimity. Whatever — it doesn't matter. We don't need to just blindly hammer bodhichitta if that's not the step that's going to actually move our mind this week ahead. We want to get what's the actual tool that's going to help me in my life. And there are really no wrong answers.

Okay, thank you so much. Let's have a little time for discussion now.

conclusion.speaker: Kadam Kyle
conclusion.text: Or two weeks. Three weeks. Oh my gosh. Holy guacamole. Yeah, because next week is the Scent of Cherishing — and then after that is empowerment bonanza, and then we'll be back on the 15th. So anyone have anything they'd like us to get up to over the three weeks ahead?

conclusion.speaker: David
conclusion.text: So Fran and I were talking about just being really honest about looking at our mind. I feel like sometimes I sort of alternate between two modes: denying that there are delusions happening, and then when I do look at them, it's really painful and I get discouraged. So just trying to be really happy to take a look at what's going on there, really focus on something small, and try to rack up a couple little wins throughout the week. Or at least being happy to try and fail. But doing it in kind of an honest, humble way.

conclusion.speaker: Kadam Kyle
conclusion.text: It's lovely, David. Yeah. Thank you so much.

conclusion.speaker: Anne
conclusion.text: I'm kind of adding to what David said since we have three weeks. I'm thinking — I don't really know what my low-hanging fruit is. So maybe I could just start with some really serious surveillance. Like, really writing down every day what's annoying me, or hurting me, or what I'm craving. And just be super detailed about it in a fun way — a discovery thing. I could spend a whole week just doing that. And I'd still have two weeks to attack the thing I've identified as the main culprit. That would be fun for me.

conclusion.speaker: Kadam Kyle
conclusion.text: Yeah, I love it. Do a little reconnaissance on the ground. Yeah. I agree — there are a lot of really interesting areas of inquiry. And to some degree, people can practice for a very, very long time and not actually solve those little basic problems that happen day by day.

conclusion.speaker: Anne
conclusion.text: And that's what life is made out of.

conclusion.speaker: Kadam Kyle
conclusion.text:
Yeah. And it's a little scary from one point of view. But it's also very humbling and helpful to know. It's like, okay, that's actually where our practice is at. That's where the magic really happens.

I think there's a big project here — from one point of view, really important, really interesting. And I think it's going to make us better practitioners and teachers to really get in there and gnaw on some of this good stuff.

I'll just guide a little meditation now — a little dedication. We can think through the virtues we've collected through practicing, meditating, discussing.
